ingredients.name: Rice flour (plain, not glutinous)
ingredients.notes: about 2 cups; long-grain white rice flour, not Japanese-style glutinous rice flour

ingredients.name: Active dry yeast
ingredients.notes: traditionally palm toddy is used instead of yeast, giving a more tangy, fermented flavour

ingredients.name: Warm water
ingredients.notes: for mixing the initial dough-like paste; added gradually

ingredients.name: Coconut milk
ingredients.notes: added after the overnight fermentation, gradually until the right consistency is reached

ingredients.name: Sugar
ingredients.notes: added after fermentation, not before, as sugar can interfere with the rise

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.notes: added after fermentation, not before, as salt can interfere with the rise

ingredients.name: Oil
ingredients.notes: for greasing the hopper pan between hoppers

steps.instruction: The night before serving (about 18-20 hours ahead), mix the rice flour, yeast, and warm water into a very thick, dough-like paste using a spoon or fork. Do not add sugar or salt at this stage. Cover and leave in a warm place to ferment for 18-20 hours, until small bubbles appear on the surface and the paste has risen slightly.

After fermentation, add the sugar and coconut milk gradually, mixing to form a smooth batter. Add the coconut milk a little at a time -- you may need slightly less or more than the amount listed, depending on the flour. The batter should be thinner than pancake batter, similar to a runny crepe batter.
Stir in the salt last. Cover the batter again and let it rest for a further 30 minutes before cooking.
Heat a hopper pan (appachatti) over medium-high heat. Lightly grease with a little oil using a paper towel or brush -- only a thin film is needed, especially on a non-stick pan.
Once the pan is hot, pour in a small ladleful of batter. Immediately lift the pan and swirl it in a circular motion to spread the batter thinly up the sides, leaving a thicker pool in the centre.
Cover the pan with a lid and let the hopper cook for about 2-4 minutes, until the edges turn golden, lacy, and crisp, while the thicker centre stays soft and spongy.
Gently loosen the edges with a spatula or your fingers and lift the hopper out. Repeat with the remaining batter, re-greasing the pan lightly between hoppers if needed.
Serve warm, plain or with sugar, alongside coconut sambol, lunu miris, or any curry.

source_site: hungrylankan.com, cross-checked against greatcurryrecipes.net, joyofeatingtheworld.com, srilankafoods.com, eggs.ca, and authenticworldfood.com for fermentation timing and batter consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; very strong agreement on the long fermentation as essential to authentic flavour, and on adding sugar/salt only after fermentation
notes: The total_time_min reflects the full 18-20 hour fermentation period required for authentic flavour, even though active hands-on time is well under an hour; quicker versions using only a few hours of fermentation exist but produce a milder, less tangy result. Traditionally, palm toddy (a fermented coconut sap drink) was used instead of commercial yeast, contributing to the dish's distinctive tang -- modern home recipes substitute yeast for convenience. A genuine hopper pan (appachatti), a small bowl-shaped pan with a lid, is important for achieving the dish's characteristic bowl shape with crisp lacy edges and a soft centre; a small wok can substitute in a pinch but won't produce quite the same shape. This batter is also the base for egg hoppers (sl_040) and several other variants such as sweet hoppers (pani appa) and steamed hoppers (wandu appa).
